segments.say: Lesson 14. Back-of-Envelope Math & the Interview Framework. Q P S, storage and bandwidth estimates in 2 minutes, plus a 45-minute structure that always works.

Back-of-the-envelope estimation is quick rough maths (requests per second, storage, bandwidth) to size a system. Plus the step-by-step structure for a 45-minute design interview. Here is an analogy. Before planning a wedding you estimate guests, food and hall size. Not exact, but enough to know whether you need a hall for 100 or 1,000.

Why does this matter? Interviewers expect quick estimates early, and they justify your later choices. A few key words. Q P S: Queries (requests) per second. D A U: Daily active users. Peak: Busiest moment, often 2–3 times average. Read:write ratio: How read-heavy the system is.
Estimating a Twitter-like app. Start with stated assumptions. Round aggressively; interviewers care about the method.
Seconds per day about 86,400 about 10 to the 5. 600M writes/day ÷ 10 to the 5 about 6,000 writes/sec. Peak about 2–3 times leads to ~15k.
Reads about 300k/sec: read-heavy at 50:1. This tells you caching and fan-out strategy matter most.
Text: ~600 G B/day leads to ~220 T B/year before replication ( times 3) and media (much more). That's distributed storage and sharding territory.
Memorize: 1M requests/day about 12 Q P S. 1 char about 1 byte. 1 image about 200 K B–2 M B. 1 min of H D video about 50–100 M B.
45-minute interview structure. Requirements: who uses it, core features (pick 3), scale, latency, consistency, availability. Ask, don't assume.
Estimates: Q P S (read versus write), storage, bandwidth. These justify your choices later.
A P I & data model: 3–5 endpoints and the main entities and keys.
High-level design: client leads to L B leads to services leads to cache/D B/queue. Get a working end-to-end design first.
Deep dives: the hardest parts (fan-out, hot keys, consistency, sharding). Let the interviewer steer.
Wrap-up: bottlenecks, failure modes, monitoring, what you'd do at 10 times scale. Name trade-offs explicitly.

Numbers to keep in your pocket. 1 day about 86,400 s about 10 to the 5 s, 1 month about 2.5M s, 1 year about 3 times 10 to the 7 s. 1M/day about 12/s, 100M/day about 1.2k/s, 1B/day about 12k/s. A single well-tuned D B: ~1k–10k simple Q P S. Redis: ~100k ops/s per node. A modern server: tens of thousands of H T T P req/s for simple endpoints.

What interviewers score. Clarifying requirements before designing. A clear, working high-level design. Identifying bottlenecks yourself and going deep. Trade-off reasoning ("I chose X over Y because. "). Communication: think out loud, check in, manage time.

Common mistakes. Jumping into the database choice in minute one. Over-engineering (Kafka plus microservices for 100 users). Never mentioning failure, monitoring or trade-offs. Silent drawing. Narrate your thinking.

Opening line that works. "Before designing, let me clarify the scope: who are the users, which features are must-haves, and what scale and latency are we targeting? Then I'll do quick estimates, sketch the A P I and data model, draw a high-level design, and we can go deep on the parts you care most about.".

A likely interview question: What's your system design approach? A strong answer: Requirements (functional and non-functional), estimates, A P I and data model, high-level design, deep dives on bottlenecks, then trade-offs, failure modes, monitoring and scaling, communicating throughout.
That's it for Back-of-Envelope Math & the Interview Framework. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
